title: Mosley v. General Motors Corp. (1974)
summary: Employees alleging injury from a common discriminatory policy could join their claims even though their individual employment experiences differed.
notes:
Compare Wal-Mart carefully. Mosley addresses Rule 20 joinder of named plaintiffs; Wal-Mart addresses proof required for a very large representative class under Rule 23.

Ten Black employees sued General Motors and the UAW under Title VII after EEOC reasonable-cause findings; the district court severed the claims into ten separate actions, and the Eighth Circuit (497 F.2d 1330) held that a companywide policy of discrimination is a single series of transactions and that the differing effects on each plaintiff are immaterial to Rule 20 joinder.

sections.Parties: Ten Black employees sued General Motors and their union concerning alleged employment discrimination.
sections.Material Facts: The employees worked in differing circumstances and alleged different forms of adverse treatment. Their complaints connected those experiences to a companywide discriminatory policy and related union conduct. The asserted common policy, rather than identical jobs or identical employment decisions, supplied the proposed link among their claims.
sections.Procedural History: The district court separated the employees’ actions. The Eighth Circuit reversed the restrictive joinder ruling and remanded.
sections.Issue: Did the allegations satisfy Rule 20’s transaction-or-series and common-question requirements?
sections.Holding: Yes. The alleged common discriminatory policy provided a sufficient relationship for permissive joinder.
sections.Reasoning: The court applied a flexible understanding of transactions and common questions. A policy operating across multiple employment decisions can connect claims without making every factual or remedial issue identical. Joint litigation could examine that shared issue while separate management of individual matters remained available. The ruling allowed the named plaintiffs to litigate together; it did not authorize them to represent absent persons without satisfying Rule 23.

learning.why: Employees alleging injury from a common discriminatory policy could join their claims even though their individual employment experiences differed.

topics.cp-permissive-joinder: A claimed companywide discriminatory policy supplied a transaction-series connection among different employees. A shared question about the challenged policy could support joinder despite differences in individual events.
topics.cp-joinder-class-distinction: Permissive joinder and certification of an absent-member class have different requirements.
topics.cp-judicial-discretion: Mosley allows related employees’ claims to proceed together while preserving the trial court’s power to manage prejudice and order appropriate separate proceedings.
topics.cp-transaction: The Eighth Circuit adopted the 'logically related' reading of 'same transaction or occurrence' for Rule 20.
topics.cp-frcp-20: The case construes the two requirements of Rule 20(a) and rejects severance under Rule 20(b) on this record.

mnemonic.rationale: Ten workers, one employer, one action
